analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on investment gains to 15% and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 14, 1990, and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the maximum tax rate on long-term capital gains — profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets held over a year — from roughly 28-34 percent down to 15 percent, with a 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers. It would also have let investors raise the 'cost' of their assets to account for inflation before calculating any taxable gain. Because most capital gains go to the wealthiest households and to corporations, the main effect would have been a large tax cut concentrated at the top, with the lost revenue made up by other taxpayers or by borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations with large unrealized gains: people selling stocks, business property, or companies would pay a 15 percent top rate instead of the much higher rate then in law, and the 7.5 percent rate would apply to gains earned by low- and middle-income taxpayers. Holders of stock and business assets held more than a year could also subtract inflation from their taxable gain, and individual investors could inflation-adjust the $3,000 annual cap on deductible capital losses.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the individual and corporate capital gains tax rate at 15 percent, down from roughly 28-34 percent.
Sets a 7.5 percent capital gains rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers.
Indexes the basis of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year, so inflation would no longer count as taxable gain.
Indexes the $3,000 and $1,500 annual limits on individual capital-loss deductions to inflation.
Reduces the alternative minimum tax rate applied to capital gains to 15 percent.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally: the revenue given up by the rate cut and indexing would have to be replaced through other taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing. Because capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households and profitable corporations, the tax savings would flow overwhelmingly to them while the cost is spread across everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The benefits are concentrated: capital gains accrue mainly to high-income households and corporations, so a rate cut to 15 percent is worth the most to them, while the lost federal revenue is borne by all taxpayers through other taxes or added borrowing.
The bill contains no offsetting revenue provisions; every dollar of reduced tax on gains would add to the deficit or require cuts or tax increases elsewhere.

Supporters would argue that taxing inflationary gains is unfair and that high rates discourage investment and the sale of businesses; the bill's indexing provision responds to that concern, but combining indexing with a deep rate cut compounds the revenue loss.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real fairness complaint — that inflation can be taxed as if it were profit — and its 7.5 percent rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers is a genuine, if small, concession. But the bulk of the money goes to the top: cutting the top gains rate to 15 percent and indexing asset values delivers the largest savings to those with the largest gains, with no way to pay for it in the bill itself. On balance it is a large, unfunded tax cut tilted toward the wealthiest households and corporations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Kasten introduced the bill on June 14, 1990, joined by 23 cosponsors, 22 of them Senate Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and never passed a chamber before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers, who would otherwise have had to make up the revenue lost to a large capital gains cut benefiting wealthy investors and corporations. Had it become law, investors and corporations with big gains would have been the winners.

for.name: Sen. Robert W. Kasten Jr.
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, proposing a 15 percent capital gains rate and inflation indexing of assets.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 101st Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 22 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, compared with 1 of 55 Senate Democrats, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of appreciated stock and business assets
industries.note: The bill would have cut their tax rate on gains to 15 percent and let them erase inflation from taxable gains — savings concentrated among the wealthiest households and profitable corporations, funded by the general taxpayer.
A 15 percent corporate capital gains rate and reduced minimum tax on gains would have cut taxes on corporate asset sales, with the revenue loss borne by the broader tax base.
The bill's title targets venture capital; a 15 percent rate plus inflation indexing would have raised after-tax returns on the kind of long-held equity stakes that produce venture capital profits.
The bill includes pass-through rules so funds, trusts, and partnerships could pass inflation indexing on to their investors, extending the benefit through the investment industry.
